text: unit wall type and insulation level The applicability logic states that only uninsulated wood stud walls are eligible for drill-and-fill insulation, whereas all dwelling units with an infiltration rate of 6 ACH50 or higher are eligible for advanced air sealing. This logic is clearly reflected in the results: uninsulated wood stud walls show an average site energy savings of 32%. All other wall type and insulation combinations show site energy savings ranging from 8% to 20%. Note that these results are more heavily influenced by advanced air sealing, as its applicability exceeds 90%, whereas drill-and-fill insulation applies to only about 30% of dwelling units. 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Stock-level applicable buildings only total annual site energy consumption by infiltration level Figure 5 shows total annual site energy consumption for the stock level before and after the upgrade. In general, dwellings with higher baseline infiltration rates achieve greater energy savings than those with lower infiltration rates. Figure 5 also shows that dwellings with low infiltration levels have relatively low stock level energy consumption. Figure 6 shows the average percentage of site energy savings per dwelling unit at different infiltration rates. Figure 6. Average applicable only annual dwelling unit percentage site energy savings by baseline infiltration rate Again, Figure 6 shows that dwellings with higher baseline infiltration rates achieve greater energy savings, exceeding 40% when the baseline infiltration is 50 ACH50. This trend continues down to 10 ACH50 but changes when infiltration rates fall below 10 ACH50. Infiltration rates of 2–5 ACH50 have a higher percentage of savings than rates of 6–8 ACH50. This is likely due to 2-5 ACH50 dwelling units having a lower annual site energy than other buildings, as seen in Figure 5, so any change to the site energy consumption results in a higher percentage change even if the absolute change is small. 18 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 7 shows the average annual site energy consumption per dwelling unit by vintage. Infiltration rates depend on vintage, so there is some correlation in the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline samples: older homes generally have higher infiltration rates and are more likely to have uninsulated walls. Figure 7. Average annual site energy consumption per dwelling unit by vintage for applicable dwelling units only In general, older homes use more energy and achieve greater energy savings. This trend appears in the following figures as well. The oldest homes, built before 1940, have an average energy savings of 32%, while the newest homes have an average energy savings of only 9%.
